claim: Abnormalities in nucleic acid processing are associated with the development of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD).
source: Abnormalities in nucleic acid processing are associated with the development of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD).
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about ALS/FTD pathogenesis.

claim: Mutations in Matrin 3 (MATR3) cause familial ALS/FTD.
source: Mutations in Matrin 3 (MATR3), a poorly understood DNA- and RNA-binding protein, cause familial ALS/FTD
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature throughout the manuscript.

claim: MATR3 pathology is a feature of sporadic ALS disease.
source: MATR3 pathology is a feature of sporadic disease
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies mentioned later in the manuscript (Dreser et al., 2017; Tada et al., 2018).

claim: MATR3 dysfunction is integrally linked to ALS pathogenesis.
source: MATR3 pathology is a feature of sporadic disease, suggesting that MATR3 dysfunction is integrally linked to ALS pathogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that MATR3 pathology appears in both familial and sporadic disease.

claim: Neurons are bidirectionally vulnerable to MATR3 levels.
source: Using a rat primary neuron model to assess MATR3-mediated toxicity, we noted that neurons were bidirectionally vulnerable to MATR3 levels
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing toxicity from both overexpression and knockdown of MATR3.

claim: Pathogenic MATR3 mutants display enhanced toxicity compared to wild-type MATR3.
source: pathogenic MATR3 mutants displaying enhanced toxicity
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: MATR3's zinc finger domains partially modulate toxicity.
source: MATR3's zinc finger domains partially modulated toxicity
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that ZF2 deletion partially rescues MATR3 overexpression toxicity (Figure 3C).

claim: Elimination of MATR3's RNA recognition motifs has no effect on neuronal survival.
source: elimination of its RNA recognition motifs had no effect on survival
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data in Figure 3E showing no significant difference in toxicity for RRM deletion mutants.

claim: Elimination of MATR3's RNA recognition motifs facilitates its self-assembly into liquid-like droplets.
source: elimination of its RNA recognition motifs had no effect on survival, instead facilitating its self-assembly into liquid-like droplets
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing formation of intranuclear granules upon RRM2 deletion (Figure 3D) and FRAP experiments demonstrating liquid-like properties (Figure 5).

claim: Cytoplasmic MATR3 redistribution mitigates neurodegeneration.
source: cytoplasmic MATR3 redistribution mitigated neurodegeneration
evidence: This is supported by survival data showing that deletion of the nuclear localization signal (∆pNLS4N) reduces MATR3-dependent toxicity (Figure 6E).

claim: Nuclear MATR3 mediates toxicity.
source: suggesting that nuclear MATR3 mediates toxicity
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that forcing MATR3 into the cytoplasm reduces toxicity.

claim: ALS is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder resulting in the death of upper and lower motor neurons.
source: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder resulting in the death of upper and lower motor neurons (Charcot and Joffroy, 1869).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ALS, supported by a historical citation.

claim: RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) are integrally involved in the pathogenesis of ALS.
source: Mounting evidence indicates that RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) are integrally involved in the pathogenesis of ALS (Taylor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The majority (>95%) of ALS patients display cytoplasmic mislocalization and deposition of TDP-43 in affected tissue.
source: The majority (>95%) of ALS patients display cytoplasmic mislocalization and deposition of the RBP TDP-43 (TAR DNA/RNA-binding protein of 43 kDa) in affected tissue (Neumann et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Over 40 different ALS-associated mutations have been identified in the gene encoding TDP-43.
source: Moreover, over 40 different ALS-associated mutations have been identified in the gene encoding TDP-43
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Mutations in several different RBPs have been linked to familial ALS.
source: mutations in several different RBPs have been similarly linked to familial ALS (Kabashi et al., 2008; Kwiatkowski et al., 2009; Vance et al., 2009; Barmada and Finkbeiner, 2010a; Ticozzi et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: ALS-associated mutations often cluster in intrinsically disordered domains that facilitate reversible liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS).
source: These mutations often cluster in intrinsically disordered domains that facilitate reversible liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), thereby creating ribonucleoprotein granules important for RNA processing, shuttling of mRNAs to sites of local translation, or sequestration of transcripts during stress.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the properties of ALS-associated RBP mutations.

claim: Pathogenic mutations in genes encoding TDP-43, FUS, and TIA1 shift the equilibrium towards irreversible phase separation and formation of cytoplasmic aggregates.
source: Pathogenic mutations in the genes encoding TDP-43 and related RBPs, including FUS and TIA1, shift the equilibrium towards irreversible phase separation and the formation of cytoplasmic aggregates analogous to those observed in post-mortem tissues from patients with ALS (Johnson et al., 2009; Patel et al., 2015; Gopal et al., 2017; Mackenzie et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The downstream implications of abnormal LLPS on RNA misprocessing, RBP pathology, and neurodegeneration in ALS are unknown.
source: The downstream implications of abnormal LLPS on RNA misprocessing, RBP pathology, and neurodegeneration in ALS are unknown, however.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: MATR3 is a DNA- and RNA-binding protein with wide-ranging functions in nucleic acid metabolism.
source: Matrin 3 (MATR3) is a DNA- and RNA-binding protein with wide-ranging functions in nucleic acid metabolism including gene transcription, the DNA damage response, splicing, RNA degradation, and the sequestration of hyperedited RNAs (Belgrader et al., 1991; Hibino et al., 2000; Zhang and Carmichael, 2001; Salton et al., 2010; Coelho et al., 2015; Rajgor et al., 2016; Uemura et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The S85C mutation in MATR3 leads to autosomal dominant distal myopathy with vocal cord and pharyngeal weakness.
source: The S85C mutation in MATR3 leads to autosomal dominant distal myopathy with vocal cord and pharyngeal weakness (Feit et al., 1998; Senderek et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Several MATR3 mutations have been identified in individuals with ALS and frontotemporal dementia (FTD).
source: A more recent report reclassified a subset of patients with this diagnosis as having ALS and noted several additional MATR3 mutations in individuals with ALS and frontotemporal dementia (FTD)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature mentioned in the context.

claim: MATR3 belongs to a family of genes implicated in familial ALS, FTD, and myopathy that also includes TIA1, VCP, p62/SQSTM1, hnRNPA1, and hnRNPA2/B1.
source: placing MATR3 in a family of genes implicated in familial ALS, FTD, and myopathy. This family also includes TIA1, VCP, p62/SQSTM1, hnRNPA1, and hnRNPA2/B1, mutations in which lead to multisystem proteinopathy characterized by variable involvement of muscle and bone in addition to the central nervous system (Hocking et al., 2002; Fecto et al., 2011; Kimonis et al., 2008; Johnson et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2013; Klar et al., 2013; Johnson et al., 2014; Mackenzie et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: A total of 13 pathogenic MATR3 mutations have been identified.
source: A total of 13 pathogenic MATR3 mutations have now been identified, most of which result in amino acid substitutions within disordered stretches of the MATR3 protein (Figure 1A) (Millecamps et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2015a; Origone et al., 2015; Leblond et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2016; Marangi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Most pathogenic MATR3 mutations result in amino acid substitutions within disordered stretches of the MATR3 protein.
source: A total of 13 pathogenic MATR3 mutations have now been identified, most of which result in amino acid substitutions within disordered stretches of the MATR3 protein (Figure 1A) (Millecamps et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2015a; Origone et al., 2015; Leblond et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2016; Marangi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1A with disorder prediction.

claim: Post-mortem analyses demonstrated MATR3 pathology in patients with sporadic ALS and familial disease due to C9orf72 hexanucleotide expansions and FUS mutations.
source: Additionally, post-mortem analyses demonstrated MATR3 pathology—consisting of cytoplasmic MATR3 accumulation as well as strong nuclear immunostaining—in patients with sporadic ALS and familial disease due to C9orf72 hexanucleotide expansions and FUS mutations (Dreser et al., 2017; Tada et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MATR3 pathology consists of cytoplasmic MATR3 accumulation as well as strong nuclear immunostaining.
source: Additionally, post-mortem analyses demonstrated MATR3 pathology—consisting of cytoplasmic MATR3 accumulation as well as strong nuclear immunostaining—in patients with sporadic ALS and familial disease due to C9orf72 hexanucleotide expansions and FUS mutations (Dreser et al., 2017; Tada et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MATR3 may be a common mediator of disease even in those without MATR3 mutations.
source: Together, these observations suggest that MATR3 may be a common mediator of disease even in those without MATR3 mutations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of MATR3 pathology in sporadic and non-MATR3 familial cases.

claim: MATR3-EGFP expressing neurons exhibited a higher risk of death compared to neurons expressing only EGFP (HR = 1.48).
source: MATR3-EGFP expressing neurons exhibited a higher risk of death compared to neurons expressing only EGFP, as quantified by the hazard ratio (HR) (HR = 1.48; EGFP n = 1286, MATR3-EGFP n = 1183; ***p<2×10−16, Cox proportional hazards).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Transfection of neurons with MATR3-EGFP resulted in a 2.8-fold increase in anti-MATR3 immunoreactivity over untransfected cells.
source: Transfection of neurons with MATR3-EGFP resulted in a 2.8-fold increase in anti-MATR3 immunoreactivity over untransfected cells (MATR3-EGFP n = 133, untransfected n = 136, EGFP n = 113, ****p<0.0001, one-way ANOVA with Tukey's post-hoc test).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: GFP fluorescence is directly proportional to anti-MATR3 reactivity on a single-cell basis.
source: On a single-cell basis, GFP fluorescence is directly proportional to anti-MATR3 reactivity (p<0.0001, r2 = 0.90; linear regression).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Higher EGFP expression is associated with a protective effect that plateaus at ~1500 arbitrary units.
source: Penalized spline modeling confirmed a protective effect associated with higher EGFP expression that plateaus at ~1500 arbitrary units (AU); (p=5.3×10−6, penalized spline regression).
evidence: This is supported by penalized spline analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: High MATR3-EGFP levels are associated with a significant increase in risk of death.
source: However, penalized spline analysis showed no relationship between expression and survival at low and medium expression but a significant increase in risk of death with high MATR3-EGFP levels (p=0.012; penalized spline regression).
evidence: This is supported by penalized spline analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: All four disease-associated MATR3 mutations (S85C, F115C, P154S, T622A) display a significant increase in toxicity compared to MATR3(WT)-EGFP.
source: All four displayed a modest but significant increase in toxicity over MATR3(WT)-EGFP when overexpressed in primary neurons (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Disease-associated MATR3 mutants (S85C, F115C, P154S, T622A) exhibit the same granular nuclear distribution as MATR3(WT)-EGFP in primary rodent cortical neurons.
source: Primary rodent cortical neurons expressing these mutant MATR3-EGFP constructs exhibited the same granular nuclear distribution as MATR3(WT)-EGFP, without obvious aggregation or cytoplasmic mislocalization, in accordance with prior reports (Figure 2A) (Gallego-Iradi et al., 2015; Boehringer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and citations to prior literature.

claim: siRNA targeting endogenous rat Matr3 reduced MATR3 antibody reactivity by approximately 65%.
source: siRNA targeting the endogenous rat Matr3 reduced MATR3 antibody reactivity by approximately 65% (scrambled siRNA, n = 576; anti-Matr3 siRNA, n = 508; p<0.0001, two-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Neurons transfected with anti-Matr3 siRNA displayed a higher risk of death compared to those transfected with scrambled siRNA (HR = 1.20).
source: Neurons transfected with anti-Matr3 siRNA displayed a higher risk of death compared to those transfected with scrambled siRNA (HR = 1.20; scrambled siRNA, n = 2507; anti-Matr3, n = 2623; ***p=2.05×10−8, Cox proportional hazards).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Neurons are vulnerable to both increases and decreases in MATR3 levels and function.
source: These data suggest that neurons are vulnerable to both increases and decreases in MATR3 levels and function
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both overexpression and knockdown of MATR3 increase the risk of neuronal death.

claim: Pathogenic MATR3 mutations may elicit neurodegeneration via gain- or loss-of-function mechanisms, or through elements of both.
source: further, pathogenic MATR3 mutations may elicit neurodegeneration via gain- or loss-of-function mechanisms, or through elements of both.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed toxicity from both overexpression of mutants and knockdown of endogenous MATR3.

claim: MATR3 has two zinc-finger (ZF) domains of the C2H2 variety, which bind DNA but may also recognize RNA and/or mediate protein-protein interactions.
source: MATR3 has two zinc-finger (ZF) domains of the C2H2 variety, which bind DNA but may also recognize RNA and/or mediate protein-protein interactions (Brayer et al., 2008; Burdach et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Deletions of ZF1, ZF2, or both had no observable effect on MATR3-EGFP localization.
source: Deletions of ZF1, ZF2, or both had no observable effect on MATR3-EGFP localization (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: ZF1 deletion by itself did not significantly alter toxicity compared to full-length MATR3-EGFP.
source: ZF1 deletion by itself did not significantly alter toxicity compared to full-length MATR3-EGFP.
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ZF2 deletion, either in isolation or combined with ZF1 deletion, partially rescued MATR3-EGFP overexpression toxicity.
source: In contrast, ZF2 deletion, either in isolation or combined with ZF1 deletion, partially rescued MATR3-EGFP overexpression toxicity (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Deletion of RRM1 failed to affect MATR3-EGFP localization.
source: While deletion of RRM1 failed to affect MATR3-EGFP localization
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Deletion of RRM2 results in redistribution of MATR3-EGFP into intranuclear granules in a subset of transfected neurons.
source: we noted a striking redistribution of MATR3(∆RRM2)-EGFP into intranuclear granules in a subset of transfected neurons (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Deletion of RRM1 in combination with RRM2 produces the same phenotype as RRM2 deletion alone.
source: Deletion of RRM1 in combination with RRM2 produced the same phenotype, suggesting that RRM2 normally prevents such redistribution.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: RRM2 normally prevents redistribution of MATR3 into intranuclear granules.
source: Deletion of RRM1 in combination with RRM2 produced the same phenotype, suggesting that RRM2 normally prevents such redistribution.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RRM2 deletion causes granule formation.

claim: Nuclear granules formed by MATR3(∆RRM2)-EGFP and MATR3(∆RRM1/2)-EGFP are uniformly spherical in shape.
source: These nuclear granules formed by MATR3(∆RRM2)-EGFP and MATR3(∆RRM1/2)-EGFP were uniformly spherical in shape
evidence: This is based on microscopy observations shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The presence of MATR3(∆RRM2)-EGFP and MATR3(∆RRM1/2)-EGFP granules is accompanied by a reduction in the intensity of diffusely-distributed MATR3 within the nucleus.
source: their presence was accompanied by a reduction in the intensity of diffusely-distributed MATR3 within the nucleus, suggesting that they represent hyperconcentrated MATR3 puncta.
evidence: This is based on microscopy observations.

claim: MATR3(∆RRM2)-EGFP and MATR3(∆RRM1/2)-EGFP granules represent hyperconcentrated MATR3 puncta.
source: their presence was accompanied by a reduction in the intensity of diffusely-distributed MATR3 within the nucleus, suggesting that they represent hyperconcentrated MATR3 puncta.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of reduced diffuse signal accompanying granule formation.

claim: RNA recognition by MATR3 is largely driven by RRM2.
source: Evidence from previous studies indicates that RNA recognition by MATR3 may be largely—but not solely—driven by RRM2 (Hibino et al., 2006; Salton et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RNA binding normally keeps MATR3 diffuse by preventing an intrinsic tendency for self-association.
source: Consistent with this, our finding that RRM2 deletion induces the formation of nuclear condensates suggests that RNA binding normally keeps MATR3 diffuse by preventing an intrinsic tendency for self-association.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that deletion of the RNA-binding domain leads to granule formation.

claim: MATR3(∆RRM2)-EGFP and MATR3(∆RRM1/2)-EGFP do not colocalize with markers of nucleoli, nuclear speckles, or PML bodies.
source: We detected no colocalization of MATR3(∆RRM2)-EGFP or MATR3(∆RRM1/2)-EGFP with markers of nucleoli, nuclear speckles, or PML bodies (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: MATR3 lacking its RRM2 does not join nucleoli, nuclear speckles, or PML bodies.
source: indicating that MATR3 lacking its RRM2 does not join these organelles.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of colocalization with markers of these structures.

claim: There was no associated change in the toxicity of MATR3-EGFP lacking RRM1, RRM2, or both in comparison to MATR3(WT)-EGFP.
source: Despite the dramatic shift in MATR3-EGFP distribution with RRM2 deletion, there was no associated change in the toxicity of MATR3-EGFP lacking RRM1, RRM2, or both in comparison to MATR3(WT)-EGFP (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: For other ALS/FTD-associated RBPs, the ability to bind RNAs is a key mediator of overexpression toxicity.
source: This finding stands in contrast to what has been observed for other ALS/FTD-associated RBPs, for which the ability to bind RNAs is a key mediator of overexpression toxicity (Elden et al., 2010; Daigle et al., 2013; Ihara et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: 76.1% of neurons transfected with MATR3(∆RRM2)-EGFP displayed nuclear granules 24 hr after transfection.
source: We therefore utilized this CV threshold to assess the frequency of nuclear granule formation in primary rodent cortical neurons, noting that 24 hr after transfection, 76.1% (2081/2734) of neurons transfected with MATR3(∆RRM2)-EGFP displayed nuclear granules
evidence: This is supported by automated analysis data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 91.2% of MATR3(∆RRM1/2)-EGFP cells displayed nuclear granules 24 hr after transfection.
source: compared to 91.2% (1590/1743) of MATR3(∆RRM1/2)-EGFP cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by automated analysis data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Nuclear granule formation occurs in a time-dependent manner in neurons expressing MATR3(∆RRM2)-EGFP.
source: We also observed the time-dependent formation of nuclear granules as neurons expressed increasing amounts of MATR3-EGFP (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Granule formation may be proportional to MATR3 expression level.
source: suggesting that granule formation may be proportional to expression level.
evidence: This is inferred from the time-dependent formation of granules as expression increases.

claim: There is no significant relationship between GFP intensity on day one and granule formation by day 3 for MATR3(∆RRM2)-EGFP.
source: Notably, we failed to observe a significant relationship between GFP intensity on day one and granule formation by day 3 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by penalized spline analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The probability of granule formation is directly proportional to the time-dependent change in MATR3(∆RRM2)-EGFP levels.
source: The probability of granule formation was directly proportional to the time-dependent change in MATR3(∆RRM2)-EGFP levels (Figure 4F)
evidence: This is supported by penalized spline analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Granule formation is favored by the rapid accumulation of MATR3(∆RRM2)-EGFP.
source: suggesting that granule formation is favored by the rapid accumulation of MATR3(∆RRM2)-EGFP.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the rate of change in expression predicts granule formation.

claim: Neurons displaying nuclear MATR3(∆RRM2)-EGFP granules fared significantly better than the population as a whole.
source: By these measures, neurons displaying nuclear MATR3(∆RRM2)-EGFP granules fared significantly better than the population as a whole
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Neurons exhibiting a diffuse distribution of MATR3(∆RRM2)-EGFP demonstrated an increased risk of death.
source: while those exhibiting a diffuse distribution demonstrated an increased risk of death (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The sequestration of RNA binding-deficient MATR3 variants into nuclear granules is associated with a survival advantage.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that diffuse MATR3 is highly neurotoxic when it cannot bind RNA. Furthermore, the sequestration of RNA binding-deficient MATR3 variants into nuclear granules is associated with a survival advantage.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that neurons with granules survive better than those with diffuse protein.

claim: Diffuse MATR3 is highly neurotoxic when it cannot bind RNA.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that diffuse MATR3 is highly neurotoxic when it cannot bind RNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that diffuse RNA-binding deficient MATR3 is more toxic than when sequestered in granules.

claim: Many RBPs reversibly undergo LLPS, involving the formation of droplets with liquid-like properties from diffuse or soluble proteins.
source: As part of their normal function, many RBPs reversibly undergo LLPS, involving the formation of droplets with liquid-like properties from diffuse or soluble proteins (Molliex et al., 2015; Murray et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Disease-associated mutations in genes encoding RBPs may promote LLPS or impair the reversibility of phase separation.
source: Disease-associated mutations in the genes encoding these proteins may promote LLPS or impair the reversibility of phase separation (Kim et al., 2013; Molliex et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2015; Conicella et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Nuclear granules formed by MATR3(∆RRM2)-EGFP and MATR3(∆RRM1/2)-EGFP exhibit dynamic properties including growing in size over time, moving freely within the nucleus, and fusing if they encounter other granules.
source: Indeed, nuclear granules exhibited dynamic properties, not only growing in size over time but also moving freely within the nucleus and fusing if they encountered other granules (Figure 5A), indicative of liquid-like behavior.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: MATR3(∆RRM1/2)-EGFP droplets show internal rearrangement consistent with liquid-like behavior.
source: Granules formed by MATR3(WT ∆RRM1/2)-EGFP displayed internal rearrangement over the course of minutes consistent with liquid-like properties
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: The recovery of MATR3(S85C ∆RRM1/2)-EGFP droplets was significantly delayed compared to wild-type.
source: The S85C mutation, however, severely slowed fluorescence recovery, suggesting reduced exchange of molecules within each droplet.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: MATR3(S85C ∆RRM1/2)-EGFP droplets displayed significantly higher viscosity in comparison to MATR3(WT ∆RRM1/2)-EGFP.
source: MATR3(S85C ∆RRM1/2)-EGFP droplets displayed significantly higher viscosity in comparison to MATR3(WT ∆RRM1/2)-EGFP (comparing to MATR3(WT ∆RRM1/2)-EGFP, n = 5: MATR3(S85C ∆RRM1/2)-EGFP, n = 5, ****p<0.0001; MATR3(F115C ∆RRM1/2)-EGFP, n = 5, p>0.9999; MATR3(P154S ∆RRM1/2)-EGFP, n = 5, p>0.9999; MATR3(T622A ∆RRM1/2)-EGFP, n = 4, p>0.9999; one-way ANOVA with Tukey's post-hoc test).
evidence: This is supported by viscosity calculations from FRAP data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: There were no differences in rates of fluorescence recovery among full-length MATR3 variants.
source: FRAP experiments involving full-length MATR3-EGFP variants showed no differences in rates of return.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5F-G.

claim: There were no differences in diffusion coefficients among full-length MATR3 variants.
source: Similarly, there were no differences in diffusion coefficients (DC) among full-length MATR3 variants (MATR3(WT)-EGFP, n = 5; MATR3(S85C)-EGFP, n = 5; MATR3(F115C)-EGFP; n = 5, MATR3(P154S)-EGFP, n = 5; MATR3(T622A)-EGFP, n = 4; p=0.17, one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by diffusion coefficient calculations from FRAP data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The S85C point mutation selectively affects the droplet properties of MATR3.
source: Our data therefore suggest that the S85C point mutation selectively affects the droplet properties of MATR3.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that S85C affects droplet viscosity but not diffusion of full-length protein.

claim: The Q66K and A72T mutations do not alter MATR3(∆RRM1/2)-EGFP droplet viscosity.
source: Unlike the S85C variant, these mutations had no effect on granule viscosity
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The S85C mutant is unique among N-terminal low-complexity domain mutations in its ability to affect the mobility of phase-separated MATR3.
source: indicating that the S85C mutant is unique among N-terminal low-complexity domain mutations in its ability to affect the mobility of phase-separated MATR3.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of S85C with Q66K and A72T mutations.

claim: Cytoplasmic inclusions composed of TDP-43 are characteristic of ALS and the majority of FTD.
source: Cytoplasmic inclusions composed of the RBP TDP-43 are characteristic of ALS and the majority of FTD (Arai et al., 2006; Neumann et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Pathogenic mutations in the gene encoding TDP-43 enhance cytoplasmic mislocalization concordant with enhanced neurotoxicity.
source: Moreover, pathogenic mutations in the gene encoding TDP-43 enhance cytoplasmic mislocalization concordant with enhanced neurotoxicity
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Reductions in cytoplasmic TDP-43 prolong neuronal survival.
source: and reductions in cytoplasmic TDP-43 prolong neuronal survival (Barmada et al., 2010b, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Multiple sequences have been associated with nuclear MATR3 localization.
source: However, since multiple sequences have been associated with nuclear MATR3 localization (Hibino et al., 2006; Hisada-Ishii et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Deletion of the N-terminal arm of NLS4 (∆pNLS4N) led to nuclear MATR3 clearance in neurons.
source: Deletion of the N-terminal arm of NLS4 (∆pNLS4N) led to nuclear MATR3 clearance in neurons.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: MATR3(∆pNLS4N)-EGFP forms granular structures in the cytoplasm and neuronal processes.
source: MATR3(∆pNLS4N)-EGFP forms granular structures in the cytoplasm and neuronal processes (white arrows).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Disrupting nuclear localization of MATR3 prevents neurotoxicity from overexpression.
source: Disrupting nuclear localization of MATR3 prevents neurotoxicity from overexpression (compared to MATR3(WT)-EGFP, n = 2459: MATR3(∆pNLS4N)-EGFP, n = 1864, HR = 0.89, ***p=0.00041, Cox proportional hazards).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Pathogenic MATR3 mutants display no difference in subcellular protein localization as assessed by automated image nuclear/cytoplasmic analysis.
source: Pathogenic MATR3 mutants display no difference in subcellular protein localization as assessed by automated image nuclear/cytoplasmic analysis (F; MATR3(WT)-EGFP, n = 789; MATR3(S85C)-EGFP, n = 462; MATR3(F115C)-EGFP, n = 596; MATR3(P154S)-EGFP, n = 524; MATR3(T622A)-EGFP, n = 657; p=0.067, one-way ANOVA)
evidence: This is supported by automated image analysis data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Pathogenic MATR3 mutants display no difference in subcellular protein localization as assessed by biochemical fractionation in transfected HEK293T cells.
source: or biochemical fractionation in transfected HEK293T cells (G).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Western blot demonstrated reduced abundance of the S85C mutant in transfected HEK293T cells.
source: Western blot demonstrated reduced abundance of the S85C mutant in transfected HEK293T cells.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The N-terminal arm of the bipartite pNLS4 is the key sequence regulating MATR3 localization in neurons.
source: Having identified the N-terminal arm of the bipartite pNLS4 as the key sequence regulating MATR3 localization in neurons
evidence: This is supported by localization data from deletion mutants shown in Figure 6.

claim: The ∆pNLS4N mutation and resulting cytoplasmic localization significantly reduced MATR3-dependent toxicity compared to MATR3(WT)-EGFP.
